Section 5 explicitly excludes importing the d≥2 scalar proof into d=1.

The ordinary centroid of each positive compact convex fiber belongs to that actual fiber. For any heavy fiber, the containing closed ambient halfspace intersects its affine fiber plane in a proper closed halfspace containing the centroid or the full plane; an empty trace is impossible. The raw contribution is at least γ_d times the fiber volume, including a fiber of volume exactly M/2. With three positive volumes no two fibers can both be at least M/2. The logic applies at any base; reversal swaps only the endpoint labels and leaves the middle point and the halfspace test unchanged.

If all fibers are strictly below M/2, reversal gives r≤s, with equality allowed. Then R>s versus R≤s exhausts the radii. In R>s the middle is largest, and 2VR^d<M is exactly R^d<r^d+s^d; thus the frozen surplus theorem gives the target at (0,b), including r=s. The upper-bound equality R^d=r^d+s^d is heavy and is already covered.

The map (z,x)↦(z,x−b−z(c−b)) is an invertible affine map preserving integer bases and translating every continuous fiber, so it preserves all raw traces and takes every closed ambient halfspace bijectively to one. At −1,0,1 the transformed fibers are a′+rK,RK,sK with a′=a+c−2b; the shear sends (0,b) to (0,0). Midpoint containment becomes a′+(r+s)K⊂2RK since K is convex. Widths scale positively and ignore translations, so 2R≥r+s. The support inequality in every direction gives a′∈(2R−r−s)K, even at equality when a′=0.

Nonnegative dilations about 0∈K nest. Minkowski addition gives A⊂(2R−s)K, with 2R−s≥r>0. In R≤s, one has 2R−s≤R≤s, so A⊂B⊂C, including equal radii or coincident sets. With the common core B, write E=V(s^d−R^d). Nonheaviness of C gives E<Vr^d; the binomial expansion of (1+1/d)^d gives γ_d≤1/2, hence E≤(1/γ_d−1)Vr^d. The denominator of the accepted normalized estimate is 2VR^d+E+Vr^d=M, so multiplying back gives the raw target γ_d M/2 at the core centroid. No replacement denominator or transfer to a different centroid occurs.

Each discarded integer fiber is null in its own d-dimensional measure, and every trace in it is a subset of that null fiber. Thus the restricted positive-fiber source and the actual source have equal raw mass in every ambient halfspace. The common-core theorem includes closed caps through the point, purely base-normal caps, and general containing caps. No noninteger slice is charged.

Exact arithmetic spot checks at d=2 in units of V: (r,R,s)=(3,5,4) has a heavy middle of exactly half mass, and (3,4,5) has a heavy endpoint of exactly half mass and midpoint saturation; both give γ_2M/(2V)=100/9. For R=s at (1,2,2), the common-core payment is 41/18≥2. For the r=s strict strip at (3,4,3), the predecessor's first bound is 137/18, exactly 1/18 above target 68/9. These checks supplement the general inequalities.

overlap.comparison: Already supplies the actual middle centroid in the nonheavy R≤s branch after the stated shear, and gives existence in the whole candidate class. For the latter in R>s, center B and write the fixed endpoint shift sum a′=(2R−r−s)k with k∈K from midpoint support. A further base shear allocates shifts (R−r)k at A and (R−s)k at C (their sum is unchanged), so the bodies equal Rk+ρ(K−k) for radii ρ=r,s,R and nest because 0∈K−k. The prior ordered/common-core theorem then gives existence; in the nonheavy R>s branch this proof selects the centroid of the sheared C as the common-core point at base zero. That centroid is (R−s)k, which need not be zero; the additional shear fixes B and its centroid. For instance take r=s=3, R=4, and a′=2k with nonzero k∈K. To center C at zero while retaining centered B would leave A=2k+3K, which is not contained in 3K. Thus this nesting implication does not certify the prescribed actual middle centroid in that strip.

Its full-mass single-fiber conclusion gives the heavy branch at the chosen centroid, with the proper/whole trace observation. It does not give the sharp target from just one fiber when all are below half.

Its proof uses a largest actual fiber centroid and obtains γ_d times that fiber's mass fraction, so it already supplies the heavy case; the fiber-count-only bound with three positive fibers gives γ_d/3.
The general three-planar-fiber theorem covers existence at γ_2/2 for d=2 after translating the base. The theorem does not select the original middle centroid.
Its actual-body theorem also gives existence at γ_2/2 for d=2 with any number of integer fibers, including null fibers, but does not specify the chosen centroid.

Equal endpoint volume, equivalently r=s here, implies existence at γ_d/2 at some point of the middle fiber, not a guarantee at the actual ordinary centroid; its unequal-volume conclusion is a different quantitative curve.

Its centroid graph result requires exact midpoint equality in volume roots, here 2R=r+s. It does not cover strict R>s≥r, and its statement selects a centroid on the graph rather than naming the middle one.
The compatible nonheavy example where every middle point fails has a nonsimplex large endpoint and a simplex middle, so it violates common homothety and is no counterexample here.

The frozen predecessor contains the stronger fixed-centroid conclusion on the strict nonheavy R>s strip. After its admission this candidate packages that conclusion with the established heavy and R≤s cases into one all-radii selection rule.
